item.title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
item.medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper
item.museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
item.lesson: Rain is nearly impossible to paint — it is transparent, everywhere, and made of motion. Hiroshige's solution, in this sheet from his final great series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, was to let the woodblock carver draw it: sheets of fine parallel lines cut at two angles, so the downpour crosshatches the darkening river. Pedestrians on the bridge bolt under hats and a shared straw mat; a lone raftsman poles on, resigned; the far bank of Atake dissolves to a gray silhouette. It is a snapshot decades before snapshots — weather as the entire subject, the 'famous view' nearly erased by it. When Japanese prints flooded into Paris, van Gogh was so possessed by this one that he copied it stroke for stroke in oils, teaching himself its flat color and diagonal daring. Hiroshige died the year after it was printed, in a cholera epidemic; his rain kept falling into the bloodstream of European modernism.
item.lookFor: Look closely at the rain itself: two separate systems of lines cross at slightly different angles — a printmaking feat requiring separate carved blocks, and the reason the shower seems to gust rather than merely fall.
